item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Thu Nov 19 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Thu Nov 19, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: "Architecture’s Forgotten Figures: The Unconventional Life and Work of Ella Briggs" — Thu Nov 19, 4:30 PM — Smith Warehouse - Bay 10
item.description:
Discover the remarkable story of Ella Briggs, a pioneering Viennese architect nearly lost to history. Trained by the Secessionists, she shaped global debates on modern living with an influential practice spanning Vienna, Berlin, London and New York. Though Nazi persecution forced her into exile and obscurity, historians recently reclaimed her groundbreaking legacy using innovative collaborative research.
Despina Stratigakos is a SUNY Distinguished Professor of Architecture at the University at Buffalo, who investigates how power, politics, and diversity intersect with design. Her work bridges academic scholarship and cultural intervention; in 2011, she partnered with Mattel to launch Architect Barbie to spark global conversations about gender equity in the field. Her 2016 book, Where Are the Women Architects?, served as a powerful indictment of a historically male-dominated profession. Most recently, her co-authored biography, Finding Ella Briggs, was named a Financial Times Best Book

item.title: Confined to a Vitrine: Indigenous Material Culture in Uruguay’s Museum of Pre-Columbian and Indigenous Art (MAPI). — Thu Nov 19, 4:30 PM — Rubenstein Library Breedlove Room 349
item.description:
In this talk, we are going to discuss the strategies used by Uruguay's Museum of Pre-Columbian and Indigenous Art (MAPI) to administer indigenous heritage. It does so by ignoring the existence of indigenous (Charrúa) activist groups that are trying to get recognition from a state that has not ratified the International Labor Organization's Convention 169 yet. The majority of Uruguayan citizens, whose beliefs are modeled by the state's dominant ideas, do not believe that there are indigenous peoples in Uruguay today. In this talk, we will discuss the predominance of colonialist narratives in the MAPI exhibitions, as well as the lack of consultation with indigenous activists, and the trivialization of the museum's mission and activities, to the point that its food tastings and musical shows (completely unrelated to indigenous art) it organizes, seem more important than, and have priority over, indigenous art
Source: Duke University

item.title: AI for Peace: A fireside chat with Branka Panic — Thu Nov 19, 5:30 PM — Sanford 223
item.description: Artificial intelligence has arrived like a tsunami - reshaping diplomacy, redistributing power, and testing the very prospects for peace. But every tsunami also reveals a new frontier: uncharted territory where the rules of statecraft have yet to be written. That is the terrain Branka Panic maps in her new book, "Foreign Policy at the AI Frontier," a guide to a world where AI ministers join cabinets, tech companies wield the influence of nation-states, satellites witness war crimes, and algorithms mediate peace. But the book is only part of the story. This fireside chat, hosted by the Duke-UNC Rotary Peace Center and Duke Center for International Development, also traces the journey behind her book: from the Balkans, a region shaped by war and its long aftermath, to Branka's years as a student in the Duke Master of International Development Policy program, to founding AI for Peace organization: a decision to build something for peace in a world that invests overwhelmingly in warfightin

item.description:
"La Bola Negra" (Javier Ambrossi & Javier Calvo, 2026, 160 min, Spain, Spanish w/ subtitles, DCP)
A bold tapestry spanning nearly a century of Spanish history, this passionate, award-winning epic from Cannes-winning directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi tells the story of three generations of men whose lives are intimately connected through desire, pain, and love.
Carlos (Milo Quifes) longs to belong in a fractured Spain. Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) finds connection across enemy lines. And Alberto (Carlos González) uncovers a long-buried family secret - one that finally gives voice to truths the past tried to erase. Combined with stunning cinematography and a grand score, the seamlessly converging storylines make for a sweeping and operatic romantic drama that delicately balances collective memory with deeply emotional personal histories. Co-written by Calvo, Ambrossi, and Alberto Conejero, and adapted from Conejero's play 'La Piedra Oscura' ('The Dark Stone').

item.title: Duke University Wind Symphony: We the People: Belonging? — Thu Nov 19, 7:30 PM — Baldwin Auditorium
item.description:
This program traces a narrative arc from the nation's founding ideals to contemporary perspectives on identity, migration, equity, and shared civic space. Through music, this performance explores belonging not as a fixed condition, but as a process shaped by history, struggle, and collective imagination. As a uniquely American ensemble rooted in civic and educational traditions, the wind symphony offers a powerful medium through which to examine the evolving meaning of belonging in the United States and within the Duke community.
For this special evening, the Duke University Wind Symphony welcomes an extraordinary group of guests: Viet Cuong, Brittany J. Green, Michele Fernandez, and Jim Obergefell. Learn more about these guests using the link on the side of this page.

Rogers Energy Access Project at Duke.
He'll discuss the growing importance of critical minerals for the energy transition, energy transitions in emerging economies, and just transitions. He will also discuss what it takes to conduct impactful applied research, translate research into policy change, and bridge the gap between evidence, policy, and implementation.

item.title: Chemistry Defense: Alexis Johnson - "Real-time Three-dimensional Electrokinetic Trapping For Prolonged Single-particle Observation and Manipulation" — Fri Nov 20, 10:00 AM — None
item.description:
Real-time Three-dimensional Electrokinetic Trapping For Prolonged Single-particle Observation and Manipulation
Single-molecule microscopy has expanded our fundamental knowledge of complex systems found in nature to reveal structural information, heterogeneity and transitional states through high temporal resolution methodology. In the Welsher Lab, 3D-SMART demonstrated its ability to gain real-time information for mechanisms of viral infection, reaction kinetics and nanoparticle characterization but tracking particles < 100 nm is challenging due to limited mechanical feedback response. To push beyond this limit, I have developed a methodology utilizing electrokinetic feedback (EKF) to trap particles.
Electric fields can manipulate charged molecules in solution with precise control so EKF has been used for single-molecule trapping. The ABEL trap has demonstrated this with single fluorescent dye trapping, at μs temporal resolution. Applications include monitoring protein dynamics

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Sat Nov 21, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Ecotones: Transitional Zones Where Ecosystems Meet — Sat Nov 21, 10:00 AM — Bynum Mill Access at Lower Haw River State Natural Area
item.description:
Friends of Lower Haw is offering a program on ecotones, transitional areas of vegetation where different natural communities meet. Examples of ecotones include transitional areas between forest and meadow, or between riverbank and water body. Our guide will be naturalist and nature photographer Jason Brown. We’ll visit transition areas where birds and wildlife can be spotted. Our guide will also talk about how past land use and land management has had an influence on the flora and fauna occurring at the Lower Haw River State Natural Area. This event is free and open to the public. All ages are welcome.

item.title: Thanksgiving: Culinary & Cultural History — Sat Nov 21, 11:00 AM — Bennett Place State Historic Site
item.description:
Did you know that our modern Thanksgiving holiday largely has its origins in 1863? During the midst of the Civil War, President Lincoln proclaimed a day of Thanksgiving on the last Thursday of November to help heal the wounds of the nation and to restore peace and union.
Lincoln ultimately decided to make this Thanksgiving proclamation at the petition of Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of Godey's Lady's Book, who had advocated for such a holiday for over 15 years! This started an annual tradition which has been celebrated nationwide ever since.
For Lincoln and the loyal states in 1863, this Thanksgiving holiday allowed Americans to give thanks for major campaign victories (like Gettysburg) that year, for continued union of the loyal states, and blessings upon those who had lost loved ones in the war.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Nov 24 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

Tue, Aug 25, 4pm-6pm American Coup: Wilmington 1898, Yoruba Richen and Brad Lichtenstein. Tue, Sep 22, 4pm-6pm How it Feels to be Free, Yoruba Richen
